title: Chapter 22: The Sunny Pair 4
content:
Chapter 22

The Sunny Pair 4

The racket was coming at him from literally everywhere.

Front and back, left and right, ceiling and floorboards—it was a surging ocean of hushed whispers, rustling giggles, and disembodied murmurs. Men, women, young and old, ringing soft and shrill alike. Fragments of stray words occasionally pierced the din, but they dissolved the second Wei Wuxian tried to latch onto them.

The white noise was dizzying.

Keeping one hand pressed firmly against his throbbing temple, Wei Wuxian reached into his pouch with the other and produced a palm-sized Compass of Evil. The needle gave a violent shudder, spun around twice, and then picked up speed until it was whirring like an absolute blur.

Having the needle freeze dead on Dafan Mountain had been odd enough, but this? Spinning endlessly without catching a single bearing was far more unsettling.

A bad feeling bloomed in his chest. Cupping his hands, he hollered, "Jin Ling!"

They’d been combing through the fortress for a while now without crossing paths with a single living soul. His calls went entirely unanswered, swallowed by the stone walls. The outer chambers had all been stripped clean, but pushing deeper into the complex, they stepped into a vaulted stone room with a heavy, pitch-black coffin resting dead center.

The box looked completely out of place sitting on the bare floor, but its woodwork was gorgeously lacquered, shaped with striking, elegant lines. Having spent half his life around burial plots, Wei Wuxian felt an immediate, bizarre wave of fond nostalgia. He couldn't resist stepping up to give the lid an appreciative tap. The wood was dense, returning a deep, solid thud. "Now that's a fine coffin."

Flanking the sides, Lan Wangji and Wei Wuxian traded a glance. Reaching out together, they shoved the lid clear.

The moment the seal broke, the background whispers spiked into an ear-splitting crescendo, crashing over Wei Wuxian's ears like a tidal wave. It felt as though hundreds of unseen eyes had been tracking their every breath in silence, gossiping behind their backs, only to lose their collective minds the second the pair dared to open the box. Wei Wuxian braced for half a dozen lethal scenarios—a blast of suffocating corpse-gas, a skeletal claw lunging for his throat, venomous slop, dark smoke, or screaming phantoms. Naturally, he’d hoped to find Jin Ling stuffed inside.

Yet nothing stirred. The box was bare.

Wei Wuxian blinked in surprise, feeling a twinge of disappointment that the brat wasn't here. Lan Wangji leaned in closer. With a metallic hum, Bichen nudged half an inch out of its scabbard, casting a pale, icy blue aura down into the shadows of the casket. Only then did they notice it wasn't completely empty. Tucked into the deepest recess was an object far smaller than any corpse.

A long sabre lay along the bottom.

It had no sheath. The hilt looked forged from solid gold, dense and undeniably heavy, balancing a long, slender blade of pristine, razor-sharp steel. Resting atop a swath of faded red silk, the blade reflected an eerie, blood-soaked sheen, radiating an unmistakable stench of raw slaughter.

A coffin built to bury a weapon instead of a body. Not a single thing about this stone fortress made sense; every step deeper into the dark only unearthed stranger secrets.

Sliding the lid back into place, they pressed forward. Several neighboring chambers housed identical coffins—the timber worn by varying decades of age, but each and every one encasing a solitary, unsheathed sabre. Reaching the final chamber, there was still no trace of Jin Ling. Wei Wuxian slid the final lid shut, a knot of worry tightening in his gut.

Noticing his grim silence, Lan Wangji paused. Setting his guqin flat across the polished coffin lid, his fingers swept across the strings, releasing a crisp sequence of notes into the dark.

It was a brief, searching melody. Pulling his hand back, Lan Wangji stared intently at the vibrating silk.

With a sudden shudder, an unplucked string gave off a clean, solitary chime.

"Inquiry?" Wei Wuxian murmured.

Inquiry was a renowned spiritual composition penned by the early masters of the Gusu Lan Clan. Unlike Evocation, which summoned a spirit using personal relics or remains, Inquiry was designed for the unknown—used when the spirit’s identity was a mystery and no physical medium existed. The performer plucked their questions into the air, and the lingering phantom’s answers were translated straight back into the chords.

A self-plucking string meant a soul lurking in this crypt had answered Lan Wangji’s summons. From here on out, player and phantom would converse entirely in zither-tongue.

Zither-tongue was the Lan Clan’s most closely guarded hereditary technique. Broad as Wei Wuxian’s occult knowledge was, he’d never cracked the code, leaving him completely unable to translate the notes. He leaned in, keeping his voice low. "Hanguang-jun, ask it where we are, what this place is for, and who built it."

Master of the craft that he was, Lan Wangji didn't need to ponder his phrasing. His fingertips brushed the strings, tossing out two or three ringing notes. A beat later, the instrument plucked itself twice in response.

Wei Wuxian leaned in eagerly. "What'd it say?"

"Unknown," Lan Wangji answered evenly.

"Huh?"

Lan Wangji’s face remained carved from stone. "It answered: 'Unknown.'"

Wei Wuxian stared at him, suddenly thrown back to that teenage classroom argument over the word whatever. Scratching his nose in defeated annoyance, he thought: Look at you, Lan Zhan. You’ve actually learned how to deadpan me.

Unshaken, Lan Wangji plucked another phrase. The strings twanged back with the exact same twin notes as before.

Recognizing the repetition, Wei Wuxian asked, "What did you ask that time?"

"Cause of death."

"If someone gets ambushed from the shadows, it makes sense they might not know how they died," Wei Wuxian mused. "Try asking if it knows who swung the blade."

Lan Wangji flicked the silk once more. The zither’s reply, predictably, was the exact same two notes: Unknown.

A soul locked inside a crypt that didn't know where it was, didn't know how it died, and didn't know who murdered it. It was Wei Wuxian’s first time running into a ghost this utterly clueless. Rubbing his chin, he suggested, "Let's change gears. Ask if it’s a man or a woman. It can't possibly blank on that."

Lan Wangji played the question. Once his hand lifted, a lower string rang out with a sharp, definitive snap.

"Male," Lan Wangji translated.

"Finally, some progress," Wei Wuxian said. "Now ask: did a teenage boy around fifteen or sixteen wander in here?"

The string chimed: Yes.

"Where is he right now?"

The instrument hesitated, pausing for a long breath before returning its answer.

"What's it saying?" Wei Wuxian pressed.

Lan Wangji’s brow furrowed. "It said... 'Right here.'"

Wei Wuxian went quiet.

'Here' obviously meant this stone fortress, but they’d just turned the place inside out without finding a hair. "Can it lie?"

"I am playing," Lan Wangji said calmly. "It cannot."

Fair enough. With Hanguang-jun running the interrogation, the spirit was pinned under absolute spiritual pressure; it had no choice but to lay down the plain truth.

Wei Wuxian began tapping along the masonry, hunting for hidden latchkeys or secret crawlspaces they might have missed. Lan Wangji turned the mystery over, then plucked out two more stanzas. When the zither answered, his expression shifted ever so slightly.

Catching the tell, Wei Wuxian spun around. "What did you ask?"

"Age, and place of origin."

Standard questions to narrow down an unidentified spirit. Wei Wuxian knew the answer had caught him off guard: "And?"

"Fifteen years old," Lan Wangji said slowly. "A native of Lanling."

The blood drained straight from Wei Wuxian’s face.

The soul answering Inquiry was Jin Ling?!

Straining his ears against the chaotic din, he thought he could faintly make out the muffled, desperate gasps of the boy, swallowed by the walls.

Lan Wangji’s fingers flew across the strings, pressing for exact coordinates. Wei Wuxian kept his eyes glued to the instrument, waiting on pins and needles.

This response ran much longer. Lan Wangji listened to the dying ring, then turned to Wei Wuxian. "Stand where you are, face southwest, and listen to the notes. With each chime, take one step forward. When the music ceases, he will be right in front of you."

Without a word, Wei Wuxian wheeled toward the southwest. Seven measured notes chimed behind him; he took seven paced strides into the gloom. Yet the space ahead remained completely empty.

The music kept playing, though the gap between each pluck stretched longer, slowing his stride. One step, two steps, three...

On the sixth stride, the strings fell dead silent.

Directly in front of him sat a solid stone wall.

The masonry was stacked with chalky gray bricks, fit together so tightly there wasn't a hairline fracture between the joints. Wei Wuxian spun back, his eyes wide. "...He’s inside the wall?!"

Shing!

Bichen cleared its scabbard in a flash of cerulean fury. Four streaks of sword-glare sliced clean through the rock in a neat grid. The two lunged forward, prying the carved stones loose to reveal a dense packing of black earth behind the masonry.

The fortress walls were double-layered—two thick skins of stone brick sandwiching a trench packed tight with compacted soil. Wei Wuxian dug his bare hands into the dirt, tearing out clods of mud until his fingers brushed against a motionless face, eyes clamped shut.

It was Jin Ling!

Buried alive in the dirt, the sudden rush of fresh air hit his lungs, triggering a violent fit of hacking and gasping. Seeing the boy draw breath, the crushing weight in Wei Wuxian’s chest finally lifted. Jin Ling had been hovering right on the edge of death; had they taken another breath to dig him out, his soul wouldn't have been caught drifting out of his flesh—he would have suffocated into a corpse.

Together, they hauled him out of the trench. But as Jin Ling’s torso pulled free of the mud, the scabbard strapped to his back caught on something deeper in the wall, dragging it out into the open.

A skeletal white arm tumbled into the torchlight!

Lan Wangji laid Jin Ling flat on the flagstones, immediately pressing two fingers to the boy’s pulse to channel spiritual energy. Wei Wuxian snatched up Bichen’s empty scabbard, using the metal tip to expertly poke and shovel through the packed soil along the skeleton's arm. Within moments, an entire human skeleton was laid bare.

Just like Jin Ling, the skeleton had been buried upright inside the wall—stark white bone framed against pitch-black dirt, a sickeningly vivid contrast. Digging further and popping off several adjacent bricks, Wei Wuxian’s scabbard struck bone again: a second skeleton.

This one hadn't fully rotted away; strips of leathery flesh still clung to the ribs, and a tangled mop of coarse black hair framed the skull. Shreds of faded pink silk clung to the frame, clearly the remains of a woman. She hadn't been buried standing; her spine was twisted forward in an awkward bend. And the reason she was bent double was because crammed right against her shins sat a third skeleton, buried in a tight, fetal crouch.

Wei Wuxian stopped digging.

Stepping back into the center of the chamber, the chaotic racket in his ears crested into a deafening, manic roar.

He didn't need to dig anymore. He was dead certain: the thick walls enclosing this entire fortress were packed wall-to-wall with human bones.

Above, below, east, west; standing, sitting, lying flat, curled into balls...

What kind of unholy tomb was this place?!
